# Sharp Non-Asymptotic Analysis of the Penalized Challenger in \(\beta\)-EB-TCI for Bernoulli Bandits

**Abstract**

Top-two algorithms are simple and effective for fixed-confidence best-arm identification, but their sharp non-asymptotic behavior is still not well understood. We study this problem for Bernoulli bandits through \(\beta\)-EB-TCI, the empirical-best top-two rule of Jourdan et al. [9], whose challenger is chosen using a Bernoulli transportation cost with a logarithmic count penalty. We prove that, after the empirical leader has become the true best arm and its sampling fraction stays close to \(\beta\), the stopping time is \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)\) up to lower-order concentration terms. We also show that, in this regime, every challenger is sampled linearly often. Thus, for the original algorithm without forced exploration, the main remaining difficulty is to control when the empirical leader becomes permanently correct. These results imply a non-asymptotic high-probability bound for all Bernoulli instances with a unique best arm. If the algorithm satisfies a finite-mean sufficient-exploration condition, the bound further yields the sharp expected sample complexity. In particular, this gives the sharp expectation result for the unguarded Bernoulli rule when all arm means are pairwise distinct, using the sufficient-exploration result of Jourdan et al. [9]. Finally, if we add a mild forced-exploration rule that contributes only \(O(\sqrt{Kt})\) pulls up to time _t_, we obtain a self-contained expected sample-complexity theorem for any number of arms under the unique-best-arm assumption. We also identify a limitation of proof strategies that try to handle equal suboptimal means through a single index-comparison argument.

### 1 Introduction

Stochastic bandits model sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At each round, a learner chooses an arm, observes a reward, and uses the accumulated data to decide what to sample next. We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification for a Bernoulli bandit with a unique best arm \(i^\star=argmax_{i\in[K]}\mu_i\). A strategy stops at a random time \(\tau_\delta\) and recommends \(\widehat{i}_{\tau_\delta}\). It is \(\delta\)-correct if

\(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\tau_\delta<\infty)=1\text{and}\mathbb{P}_\mu(\widehat{i}_{\tau_\delta}\neq i^\star)\le\delta.\)

The goal is to minimize the expected number of samples while preserving both termination and the target error probability. We use _finite-confidence_ for guarantees that hold at each fixed \(\delta\), rather than only in the asymptotic limit \(\delta\rightarrow 0\).

A central benchmark is the instance-dependent characteristic time. Algorithms such as Track-and-Stop achieve the globally optimal leading-order sample complexity by tracking an optimal allocation online [14, 4]. Doing so requires repeatedly solving or approximating a global optimization problem. In this paper, the best arm is instead assigned a prescribed asymptotic sampling fraction \(\beta\in(0,1)\). The constrained characteristic time \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) is defined so that \(1/T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) is the largest worst-case information<tbc>

Top-two algorithms provide a simpler alternative. They maintain a current leader and compare it with one challenger at a time \[16, 17, 9\]. This structure is easy to implement and has strong asymptotic guarantees. In particular, Jourdan et al. \[9\] proved asymptotic \(\beta\)-optimality--optimal leading-order complexity when the best arm receives sampling fraction \(\beta\)--for several top-two rules on bounded rewards, including the Bernoulli \(\beta\)-EB-TCI rule studied here. Non-asymptotic results with the exact leading coefficient are more limited. The closest existing analysis is the Gaussian Top-Two UCB (TTUCB) result of Jourdan and Degenne \[8\], which treats a different top-two rule and a different reward model.

We analyze the exact Bernoulli \(\beta\)-EB-TCI rule, where EB-TCI stands for Empirical-Best Transportation-Cost Index. Under the unguarded rule, the empirical-best arm is sampled with probability \(\beta\) at each round. With probability \(1-\beta\), the algorithm selects the challenger minimizing \(j\mapsto W_t(B_{t+1},j)+logN_{t,j}\). Here _W<sub>t</sub>_ is a one-sided Bernoulli generalized likelihood-ratio (GLR) statistic: when _B_<sub>_t_+1</sub> is the empirical leader, _W<sub>t</sub>(B_<sub>_t_+1</sub>_,j_) measures the evidence that separates the leader from arm _j_. The additional term log_N<sub>t,j</sub>_ favors less-sampled challengers when the evidence values are comparable. It is part of the algorithm, not an auxiliary proof term.

A finite-confidence analysis of this rule must address three coupled questions. First, how closely do the empirical GLR indices follow their counterparts computed at the true means under adaptive sampling? Second, once the true best arm becomes the persistent leader, does the penalized challenger rule continue to sample every suboptimal arm often enough? Third, how long does it take until the true best arm remains the leader and the best-arm sampling fraction is close to \(\beta\)? The stopping-rule result of Jourdan et al. \[9\] controls the probability of a wrong recommendation on runs that stop, but does not itself prove that stopping occurs. Termination and sample complexity therefore require separate control of entry into this regime, challenger sampling, and the stopping threshold.

Our first result resolves challenger sampling and stopping once the algorithm has entered the stabilized regime. By this we mean that, from some time onward, the true best arm is always the empirical leader and its sampling fraction remains in a fixed neighborhood of \(\beta\). We show that every suboptimal-arm pull count then grows linearly and that the stopping time has leading term \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)\). The proof combines a deterministic population allocation benchmark for the penalized challenger with a time-uniform comparison between empirical and population pairwise Bernoulli GLR statistics.

Our second result removes the assumption that this regime has already been reached. For the unguarded algorithm, we obtain a non-asymptotic high-probability stopping bound for every Bernoulli instance with a unique best arm. To turn this bound into an expected stopping-time guarantee, one needs _sufficient exploration_: after an almost-surely finite random time with finite expectation, every arm must have at least order \(\sqrt{t/K}\) pulls. For pairwise-distinct means, Jourdan et al. \[9\] establish this property for the unguarded tie-breaking variant covered by their analysis. This result does not automatically apply to our fixed deterministic tie-breaking convention. We therefore also study a simple exploration guard that pulls a least-sampled arm whenever some count is below \(\sqrt{t/K}\). The guard enforces sufficient exploration directly while using only \(O(\sqrt{Kt})\) pulls by time _t_.

## Contributions.

Our main contributions are:

1. **Analysis of the exact penalized challenger.** We analyze the Bernoulli GLR challenger with its logarithmic count penalty. We prove a discrete population allocation approximation for the greedy challenger counts and a time-uniform empirical-to-population bound for pairwise Bernoulli GLR statistics under adaptive sampling.<tbc>

2. **Leading-order sharpness in the stabilized regime.** Once the true best arm remains the leader and its sampling fraction stays near \(\beta\), we prove linear growth of every suboptimal-arm pull count and an upper bound with leading term \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)\). Throughout the paper, _sharp_ refers to this exact fixed-\(\beta\) leading coefficient. We do not claim optimized lower-order constants or a matching non-asymptotic lower bound.<tbc>

3. **Guarantees without assuming the stabilized regime in advance.** For the unguarded algorithm, we prove a non-asymptotic high-probability stopping bound under a unique best arm. Under finite-mean sufficient exploration, the same argument yields the expected bound. We obtain<tbc>

<tbc>the pairwise-distinct-means corollary only for the tie-breaking variant covered by Jourdan et al. \[9\]. For the guarded algorithm, we prove the expected bound for any number of arms under a unique best arm. We also identify a limitation of one natural proof route for groups of equal-mean suboptimal arms: a single pointwise comparison of two penalized indices cannot by itself give a tail bound strong enough to ensure a finite expected time to reach the stabilized regime.

## 2 Related Work

### Fixed-confidence identification and allocation tracking.

Fixed-confidence best-arm identification has progressed from elimination-style methods to information-theoretic, instance-dependent analyses \[15, 3, 1, 11\]. The characteristic-time formulation of Kaufmann et al. \[14\] and Track-and-Stop of Garivier and Kaufmann \[4\] connect lower bounds to an adaptive rule that tracks a globally optimal allocation. Methods based on Lower/Upper Confidence Bounds (LUCB), together with KL-based refinements, form another major family \[10, 12, 7\]. Our setting fixes the best-arm sampling fraction at \(\beta\) and uses local leader-challenger updates rather than tracking the full optimal allocation.

### Top-two methods.

Top-two algorithms repeatedly compare a current leader with a selected challenger. They were introduced in Bayesian form by Russo \[16\], studied in fixed-confidence settings by Shang et al. \[17\], and developed into a frequentist bounded-reward framework by Jourdan et al. \[9\]. EB-TCI is the empirical-best member of that framework. We specialize it to Bernoulli rewards and analyze the exact logarithmically penalized challenger, rather than an unpenalized rule, a Gaussian approximation, or a different top-two construction. The Gaussian TTUCB result of Jourdan and Degenne \[8\] is the closest existing non-asymptotic analysis.

### Time-uniform concentration and stopping-time tails.

Our concentration arguments build on mixture martingales and time-uniform confidence bounds, often called confidence sequences \[13, 5, 6\]. A key step converts armwise KL confidence sequences into uniform control of pairwise Bernoulli GLR statistics at the effective sample size of the two arms. Separate work has emphasized that correctness and high-probability stopping bounds do not automatically imply a sharp expected stopping time \[2\]. Our analysis reflects this distinction: we first study the algorithm in the stabilized regime, and then separately bound how long it takes to enter that regime, both in probability and in expectation. The error guarantee for the GLR stopping rule is taken from Jourdan et al. \[9\]; termination and the finite-time behavior of the challenger counts are proved here. Appendix A records the precise role of each result used from prior work.

## 3 Setting and Algorithm

We consider a Bernoulli bandit with \(K\ge 2\) arms and mean vector \(\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K)\in(0,1)^K\). We assume a unique best arm, \(i^\star=argmax_{i\in[K]}\mu_i\). After _t_ pulls, _N<sub>t,i</sub>_ denotes the number of times arm _i_ has been sampled, and \(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}\) denotes its empirical mean. Unless stated otherwise, all finite-set argmax and argmin operations use one fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule; the experiments use the smallest-index rule. Corollary 6.5 is the only exception: it invokes a result of Jourdan et al. \[9\] for the tie-breaking convention covered by their theorem.

For \(p\in[0,1]\) and \(q\in(0,1)\), write

\(d(p,q):=plog\frac{p}{q}+(1-p)log\frac{1-p}{1-q},\)

with the conventions 0log0=0 and 1log1=0. When both arguments are in (0,1), this is the Bernoulli Kullback–Leibler divergence _d(p,q_)=KL(Ber(_p),_Ber(_q_)).

We use two related evidence statistics. For any distinct arms _i_ and _j_, the symmetric two-sample generalized likelihood-ratio statistic is \(V_t(i,j):=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{N_{t,id}(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i},x)+N_{t,j}d(\widehat{\mu}_{t,j},x)\right\}.\) The value is symmetric in _i_ and _j_. Equivalently, the infimum may be taken over \[0,1\] using the standard boundary convention for Bernoulli KL. Replacing the empirical means by the true means gives the corresponding population quantity \(V_t^\mu(i,j):=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{N_{t,id}(\mu_i,x)+N_{t,j}d(\mu_j,x)\right\}.\)

The algorithm uses the following one-sided version, traditionally called the transportation cost:

\(W_t(i,j):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
V_t(i,j), & \widehat{\mu}_{t,i}\ge\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}, \\
0, & \widehat{\mu}_{t,i}<\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}.
\end{array}\right.\)

Thus evidence is counted only when the first arm has at least as large an empirical mean as the second. This is the ordered transportation cost of Jourdan et al. \[9\]. In particular, if _i_ is the empirical leader and \(j\neq i\), then _W<sub>t</sub>(i,j_)=_V<sub>t</sub>(i,j_).

For Bernoulli KL, the minimizing common mean is the sample-size-weighted pooled mean \(x_t(i,j)=\frac{N_{t,i}\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}+N_{t,j}\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}}{N_{t,i}+N_{t,j}}\) , with the same formula for \(V_t^\mu(i,j)\) after replacing empirical means by population means.

After _t_ pulls, the algorithm first identifies the empirical leader \(B_{t+1}\in argmax_{i\in[K]}\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}\) and sets the current recommendation to \(\widehat{i}_t:=B_{t+1}\). If the stopping condition is not met and no guard is active, it then chooses \(C_{t+1}\in argmin_{j\neq B_{t+1}}\left\{W_t(B_{t+1},j)+logN_{t,j}\right\},\) again with the same fixed tie-breaking rule, and pulls the leader with probability \(\beta\in(0,1)\) and the challenger with probability \(1-\beta\). Before the empirical leader is permanently correct, \(\beta\) is literally the leader-selection probability; after stabilization, it controls the sampling fraction of the true best arm.

We also study an optional _exploration guard_. It is activated whenever \(min_{i\in[K]}N_{t,i}<\sqrt{t/K}\) and then pulls a least-sampled arm instead of using the top-two decision. The leader _B_<sub>_t_+1</sub> is still defined on guarded rounds, whereas the challenger _C_<sub>_t_+1</sub> is used only on unguarded rounds. Let \(G_t^\text{tot}\) denote the number of guarded pulls made by time _t_. Throughout the paper, the _unguarded algorithm_ means the original \(\beta\)-EB-TCI rule without this modification. We use the time-dependent GLR stopping threshold of Jourdan et al. \[9\],

\(c(t,\delta)=log(1/\delta)+2log(1+t/2)+2+log(K-1).\) (3.1)

The stopping time and terminal recommendation are

\(\tau_\delta:=inf\left\{t\ge K:min_{j\neq B_{t+1}}W_t(B_{t+1},j)>c(t,\delta)\right\},\widehat{i}_{\tau_\delta}:=B_{\tau_\delta+1}.\) (3.2)

The martingale analysis of Jourdan et al. \[9\] gives the following error guarantee for this stopping rule on bounded rewards:

\(\mathbb{P}_\mu\big(\tau_\delta<\infty,\widehat{i}_{\tau_\delta}\neq i^\star\big)\le\delta\)

for any adaptive sampling rule. This statement controls the chance of a wrong recommendation on runs that stop; it does not prove that the stopping time is finite. Almost-sure termination is established separately by the stopping-time results in Sections 5-6. Combining termination with the display above gives \(\delta\)-correctness in each regime covered by our theorems. Appendix B gives the formal reduction.

**Algorithm 1** \(\beta\)-EB-TCI with GLR stopping and optional exploration guard

1: Pull each arm once.

2: **for** _t=K,K_+1_,..._ **do**

3: \(B_{t+1}\in argmax_{i\in[K]}\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}\) _fixed deterministic tie-breaking_

4: \(\widehat{i}_t\leftarrow B_{t+1}\)

5: **if** \(min_{j\neq B_{t+1}}W_t(B_{t+1},j)>c(t,\delta)\) **then**

6: stop and recommend \(\widehat{i}_t\)

7: **end if**

8: **if** the guard is enabled and \(min_{i\in[K]}N_{t,i}<\sqrt{t/K}\) **then**

9: \(I_{t+1}\in argmin_{i\in[K]}N_{t,i}\) _guarded pull_

10: **else**

11: \(C_{t+1}\in argmin_{j\neq B_{t+1}}\left\{W_t(B_{t+1},j)+logN_{t,j}\right\}\)

12: Draw \(U_{t+1}\sim Ber(\beta)\) independently of the past.

13: \(I_{t+1}\leftarrow B_{t+1}\) if _U_<sub>_t_+1</sub>=1, and \(I_{t+1}\leftarrow C_{t+1}\) otherwise.

14: **end if**

15: **end for**

## 4 Population Allocation Benchmark and Uniform GLR Control

### 4.1 A discrete penalized allocation benchmark

We first describe the population allocation benchmark used in the analysis. For a prescribed best-arm fraction \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and a suboptimal arm \(j\neq i^\star\), define \(I_j^\alpha(w)=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},x)+wd(\mu_j,x)\right\},w>0\). If arm _j_ receives asymptotic fraction _w_, then \(I_j^\alpha(w)\) is the per-round information rate for separating _i<sup>⋆</sup>_ from _j_. Allocating the remaining mass \(1-\alpha\) across all suboptimal arms gives the constrained characteristic time \(T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}=max_{w\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}} min_{j\neq i^\star} I_j^\alpha(w_j)\), where \(\Delta_{1-\alpha}=\left\{w\in(0,\infty)^{K-1}:\sum_{j\neq i^\star} w_j=1-\alpha\right\}\). Decom posing the full allocation simplex by the best-arm coordinate gives the global characteristic time

\(T^\star(\mu):=min_{\alpha\in(0,1)}T_\alpha^\star(\mu),T_\beta^\star(\mu)\ge T^\star(\mu).\)

Thus \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) quantifies the possible loss from prescribing the best-arm fraction instead of optimizing it. We keep \(\beta\) fixed throughout; we do not analyze an online estimate or adaptive choice of \(\beta\).

To connect this continuous allocation problem to integer pull counts, let _n_ denote a best-arm pull count and let _s_ denote the total pull count assigned to all other arms. For integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(s\ge K-1\), define \(\Phi_j(n,m)=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{nd(\mu_{i^\star},x)+md(\mu_j,x)\right\}+logm\), and define the discrete penalized allocation benchmark

\(\Gamma_{n,s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)=max_{m\in\{1,2,\dots\}}^{K-1:\sum_{j\neq i^\star} m_j=s}min_{j\neq i^\star}\Phi_j(n,m_j).\)

This optimization uses the true means and integer pull counts; it is therefore a population-level benchmark, not an implementable algorithm. It describes the largest possible minimum penalized index across challengers with _n_ best-arm pulls and _s_ non-best-arm pulls, including the same logarithmic penalty used by \(\beta\)-EB-TCI.

**Proposition 4.1** (Approximation of the discrete penalized benchmark)**.** _Fix a compact interval_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\)_. There exists a constant_ \(C_\mu(U)<\infty\) _such that for every_ \(n\ge 1\) _and every_ \(s\ge K-1\)_, if t=n+s,_ \(\alpha=n/t\)_, and_ \(\alpha\in U\)_, then_

\(\left|\Gamma_{n,s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)-\left(\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+logt\right)\right|\le C_\mu(U).\)

To interpret the proposition, set _t=n+s_, \(\alpha=n/t\), and _w<sub>j</sub>=m<sub>j</sub>/t_. The continuous allocation problem predicts the leading value \(t/T_\alpha^\star(\mu)\), while the count penalty contributes log_t_. Proposition 4.1 shows that integer rounding and the arm-dependent terms inside log_m<sub>j</sub>_ change this value by only \(O_\mu(1)\), uniformly when \(\alpha\) stays in a compact subset of (0,1).

### 4.2 Uniform comparison of empirical and population pairwise GLR statistics

For the analysis, define the time-uniform confidence term \(H_t(\eta):=\mathrm{log}(K/\eta)+\mathrm{loglog}(et)\) and the two-arm effective sample size \(N_{\mathrm{eff},t}(i,j):=\frac{N_{t,i}N_{t,j}}{N_{t,i}+N_{t,j}}\). This effective sample size satisfies \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{min}\{N_{t,i},N_{t,j}\}\le N_{\mathrm{eff},t}(i,j)\le\mathrm{min}\{N_{t,i},N_{t,j}\}\). The next theorem shows that the empirical pairwise GLR stays uniformly close to its counterpart computed at the true means, at the corresponding fluctuation scale.

**Theorem 4.2** (Time-uniform pairwise Bernoulli GLR approximation)**.** _There exists an instance- dependent constant_ \(C_\mu<\infty\) _such that for every_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _there is an event_ \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\) _with_ \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{G}_\eta)\ge 1-\eta\) _and, on_ \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\)_, simultaneously for all_ \(t\ge K\) _and all pairs_ \(i\neq j\),

\(|V_t(i,j)-V_t^\mu(i,j)|\le C_\mu\left(\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff},t}(i,j)H_t(\eta)}+H_t(\eta)\right).\)

The population statistic \(V_t^\mu(i,j)\) grows on the scale _N_eff_,t(i,j_), while the deviation is of order \(\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff},t}(i,j)H_t(\eta)}+H_t(\eta)\). Therefore, if both arms are sampled increasingly often, the relative error vanishes. This quantitative statement lets us transfer the population allocation bound to the adaptive empirical indices used by the algorithm.

### About the two results. Proposition 4.1 identifies the best minimum population penalized index attainable at fixed integer pull totals. A deterministic argument for the greedy challenger-count update in Appendix E relates the actual challenger counts to this benchmark. Theorem 4.2 then controls the error incurred when the true means are replaced by adaptive empirical means. Once the true best arm is the empirical leader, the one-sided statistic used by the algorithm satisfies _Wt(i⋆,j_)=_Vt(i⋆,j_). The two results can therefore be combined to lower-bound the evidence against every challenger. ## 5 Sharp Guarantees in the Stabilized Regime We first analyze the algorithm after both its leader and its best-arm sampling fraction have stabilized. Define its sampling fraction by \(\alpha_t=N_{t,i^\star}/t\). Fix a compact interval \(U\Subset(0,1)\) whose interior contains \(\beta\). We call _tU_ a _U-stabilization time_ if _B__t_+1=_i⋆_ and \(\alpha_t\in U,\forall t\ge t_U\). Thus, after a _U_-stabilization time, the true best arm remains the empirical leader and its sampling fraction stays in _U_. Throughout this section, _stabilization_ refers to this joint condition, not only to the leader identity. For an almost-surely finite random time _T_, an _upper-quantile bound_ is a function \(u_T:(0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty)\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}_\mu\left(T\le u_T(\eta)\right)\ge 1-\eta\text{for every}\eta\in(0,1].\) Equivalently, \(u_T(\eta)\) is a \((1-\eta)\)-confidence upper bound on _T_. We call the bound _summable_ if \(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}u_T(2^{-k})<\infty\). This dyadic summability condition is strong enough to integrate the tail bound and obtain a finite contribution to \(\mathbb{E}_\mu[T]\). For \(t\ge t_U\) and \(j\neq i^\star\), the challenger rule compares the empirical penalized indices _Pt(j_)=_Vt(i⋆,j_)+log_Nt,j_. Their population counterparts are \(Q_t(j)=\Phi_j(N_{t,i^\star},N_{t,j})=V_t^\mu(i^\star,j)+logN_{t,j}\). After stabilization, _B__t_+1=_i⋆_, so \(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i^\star}\ge\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}\) for every \(j\neq i^\star\) and therefore _Wt(i⋆,j_)=_Vt(i⋆,j_). For later bounds, we also use the slightly looser confidence term \(\widetilde{H}_t(\eta):=log(K/\eta)+log(et).\) **Proposition 5.1** (Uniform lower bound on evidence against all challengers)**.** _Fix a compact interval_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\) _containing_ \(\beta\) _in its interior. There exist constants_ \(C_\mu(U),\overline{C_\mu}(U)<\infty\) _such that for every_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _there is an event_ \(\mathcal{E}_\text{env}(\eta)\) _with_ \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{E}_\text{env}(\eta))\ge 1-2\eta\) _on which the following holds simultaneously for every U-stabilization time tU and every_ \(s\ge t_U\): \(min_{j\neq i^\star} Q_s(j)\ge\Gamma_{N_{s,i^\star},s-N_{s,i^\star}}^\text{disc}(\mu)-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right)-\overline{C_\mu}(U).\) _Consequently, on the same event,_ \(min_{j\neq i^\star} W_s(i^\star,j)\ge\frac{s}{T_{\alpha_s}^\star(\mu)}-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right)-\overline{C_\mu}(U).\) **Theorem 5.2** (Non-asymptotic stopping bound in the stabilized regime)**.** _Fix_ \(\beta\in(0,1)\) _and a compact interval_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\) _containing_ \(\beta\) _in its interior. Let tU be an almost-surely finite U-stabilization time. Then there exist instance-dependent constants_ \(C_{\mu,0}(U),C_{\mu,1}(U),C_{\mu,2}(U),C_{\mu,3}(U)<\infty\) _such that, for every_ \(\delta\in(0,1/2]\) _and every_ \(\eta\in(0,1/4]\)_, with probability at least_ \(1-3\eta\), \(\tau_\delta\le(1+C_{\mu,0}(U))t_U+T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)+C_{\mu,1}(U)\sqrt{log(1/\delta)\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog\frac{e}{\delta}\right)}\)
\(+C_{\mu,2}(U)\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog\frac{e}{\delta}\right)+C_{\mu,3}(U).\) _Moreover, if tU admits a summable upper-quantile bound, then there exist constants_ \(C'_{\mu,1}(U),C'_{\mu,2}(U),C'_{\mu,3}(U)<\infty\) _such that, for all_ \(\delta\in(0,1/2]\), \(\mathbb{E}_\mu[\tau_\delta]\le T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)+C'_{\mu,1}(U)\sqrt{log(1/\delta)loglog(e/\delta)}+C'_{\mu,2}(U)loglog(e/\delta)+C'_{\mu,3}(U).\) Appendix F gives the proof. The lower-order terms have four sources: the time _tU_ needed to enter the stabilized regime; fluctuations of the pairwise GLR statistics and of the best-arm sampling fraction; the uniform-in-time confidence error and inversion of the stopping threshold; and bounded discretization, penalty, and early-time effects. None changes the fixed-\(\beta\) coefficient multiplying \(log(1/\delta)\).

### What remains to be controlled. Theorem 5.2 reduces the remaining problem to controlling the _U_-stabilization time _tU_. A high-probability bound on _tU_ gives a high-probability stopping bound, while a summable upper-quantile bound gives an expected stopping-time bound. The next proposition shows why this reduction is useful: in the stabilized regime, the penalized challenger rule cannot keep any suboptimal arm under-sampled. Each suboptimal-arm pull count grows linearly after a transient determined by _tU_ and the concentration error. **Proposition 5.3** (Linear growth of every suboptimal-arm pull count in the stabilized regime)**.** _Fix a compact interval_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\) _containing_ \(\beta\) _in its interior and define_ \(\lambda_{\mu,U}:=inf_{\alpha\in U}T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}>0\)_. On the event of Proposition 5.1, simultaneously for all_ \(s\ge t_U\) _and all_ \(j\neq i^\star\), \(N_{s,j}\ge\frac{\lambda_{\mu,U}s-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right)-\overline{C_\mu}(U)-logs}{d(\mu_j,\mu_{i^\star})}.\) To translate count growth into permanent empirical separation, let _c_0_\>_0 be the universal constant from the armwise time-uniform confidence bound in Appendix D.1, and define \(r(n,\eta)=\sqrt{\frac{c_0}{2n}\left(log\frac{8K^2}{\eta}+loglog(en)\right)},\)
\(n_j(\eta)=min\left\{n\ge 1:r(n,\eta)\le\frac{\mu_{i^\star}-\mu_j}{4}\right\},n_\star(\eta)=max_{j\neq i^\star} n_j(\eta).\) Here \(n_j(\eta)\) is the number of samples needed to estimate arms _i⋆_ and _j_ to within one quarter of their mean gap. Define the first time at which all of these count requirements hold by \(t_\mathrm{sep}(\eta)=inf\left\{t\ge K:N_{t,i^\star}\ge n_\star(\eta)\text{and}N_{t,j}\ge n_j(\eta)\forall j\neq i^\star\right\}\). ## 7 Experiments

The experiments examine four questions directly connected to the analysis: (i) how observed stopping times compare with the predictor based on \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\); (ii) how performance changes with the leader- sampling probability \(\beta\); (iii) how many pulls are introduced by the guard; and (iv) what changes when the logarithmic challenger penalty is removed. These experiments are diagnostic and are not intended as a broad comparison of best-arm algorithms. All experiments use Bernoulli rewards, the stopping threshold in (3.1), and smallest-index tie-breaking.

### Protocol.

We use three representative mean vectors: `SEP5`=\[0.70,0.50,0.40,0.30,0.20\] has well-separated arms, `CLUSTER-CLOSE5`=\[0.70,0.64,0.63,0.62,0.61\] has distinct but closely clustered suboptimal arms, and `TIE-CLOSE4`=\[0.60,0.56,0.56,0.56\] has three equal-mean suboptimal arms. The evaluation grid contains three instances, \(\beta\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}\), and \(\delta\in\{10^{-4},10^{-5},10^{-6},10^{-7},10^{-8}\}\). For each setting we run both the unguarded and guarded algorithms with 200 independent replications. We compare the empirical mean stopping time with the threshold-crossing predictor

\(t_\text{pred}(\mu,\beta,\delta):=min\{t\ge K:t/T_\beta^\star(\mu)>c(t,\delta)\}.\)

This predictor is the smallest time at which the leading information \(t/T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) exceeds the same threshold used by the algorithm. Appendix H gives the full grids, random-seed policy, numerical solver, uncertainty summaries, stopping caps, and additional diagnostics. The supplementary code package provides the reproduction commands.

### Predictor agreement and sensitivity to \(\beta\).

Here, predictor agreement means closeness between the empirical mean stopping time and _t_pred. Figure 1 shows the scaling at \(\beta=0.5\). The empirical means track the threshold-crossing predictor on both `SEP5` and `TIE-CLOSE4`. Across the 45 guarded settings, the mean and maximum absolute relative errors with respect to _t_pred are 1.53% and 3.86%; for the unguarded settings, they are 1.66% and 4.20%. None of the 18,000 penalized runs reaches the 700,000-round cap or recommends a wrong arm. Figure 2 also shows that the dependence on \(\beta\) is nonmonotone and instance-specific, as predicted by \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\); the raw mean gaps alone do not determine the best choice of \(\beta\).

### Guard overhead, effect of removing the penalty, and an idealized reference.

Appendix H reports the full diagnostics. On `TIE-CLOSE4` with \(\beta=0.5\) and \(\delta=10^{-8}\), enabling the guard changes the median stopping time from 104,918 to 103,743 and the empirical 95th percentile from 134,140 to 130,792; the largest mean fraction of guarded pulls in the tested equal-mean instances is 0.0069%. Removing the penalty log_N<sub>t,j</sub>_ raises the mean stopping time from 105,593 to 188,036, with 12.8% of runs reaching the cap. The appendix also includes an idealized reference that knows the true means and tracks a globally optimal allocation. This reference is not empirical Track-and-Stop and is used only to provide scale, not to rank algorithms.

### Takeaway.

On the tested Bernoulli instances, the observed mean stopping times closely follow the predictor that combines \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) with the actual stopping threshold. The guard adds very few pulls, whereas removing the logarithmic penalty substantially worsens the equal-mean stress test. These experiments support the mechanisms analyzed here; they do not establish uniform superiority over other best-arm identification algorithms.

## 8 Conclusion

We analyzed the exact logarithmically penalized challenger in Bernoulli \(\beta\)-EB-TCI at finite confidence. In the stabilized regime, every suboptimal-arm pull count grows linearly and the stopping-time upper bound has the exact fixed-\(\beta\) leading term \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)log(1/\delta)\); lower-order constants are not optimized.

The deterministic unguarded rule has a non-asymptotic high-probability stopping bound, while its expected bound additionally requires finite-mean sufficient exploration. For pairwise-distinct means, Jourdan et al. [9] supply this property only for their tie-breaking variant. The guard supplies it for arbitrary _K_ with only \(O(\sqrt{Kt})\) guarded pulls by time _t_. The proof is Bernoulli-specific with fixed \(\beta\); extensions beyond Bernoulli rewards, online \(\beta\) adaptation, and finite-mean stabilization with tied suboptimal means remain open.

The bounded-reward result of Jourdan et al. \[9, Lemma 2\], specialized to the Bernoulli transportation cost and threshold (3.1), gives

\(N_{t,i}d(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i},\mu_i)\le c_0\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog(et)\right)\text{for all}t\ge K\text{and}i\in[K].\)

Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \(j\neq i^\star\), and _w\>_0. Define<tbc>

\(m_j^\alpha(w):=\frac{\alpha\mu_{i^\star}+w\mu_j}{\alpha+w}.\)

<tbc>By Remark B.2, the infimum in the definition of \(I_j^\alpha(w)\) is uniquely attained at \(x=m_j^\alpha(w)\), and<tbc>

\(I_j^\alpha(w)=\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},m_j^\alpha(w))+wd(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w)).\)

<tbc>**Proposition C.1** (Bernoulli population-allocation calculus)**.** _The map_ \(I_j^\alpha\) _is_ \(C^\infty\) _on_ \((0,\infty)\)_, strictly increasing, and strictly concave. More precisely,_<tbc>

\(\frac{d}{dw}I_j^\alpha(w)=d(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w))>0,\)

<tbc>_and_<tbc>

\(\frac{d^2}{dw^2}I_j^\alpha(w)=-\frac{\alpha^2(\mu_{i^\star}-\mu_j)^2}{(\alpha+w)^3m_j^\alpha(w)(1-m_j^\alpha(w))}<0.\)

<tbc>_Proof of Proposition C.1._ For \(x\in(0,1)\), let<tbc>

\(f_w(x):=\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},x)+wd(\mu_j,x).\)

<tbc>Since<tbc>

\(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}d(p,x)=-\frac{p}{x}+\frac{1-p}{1-x}=\frac{x-p}{x(1-x)},\)

<tbc>we obtain<tbc>

\(f'_w(x)=\frac{(\alpha+w)x-(\alpha\mu_{i^\star}+w\mu_j)}{x(1-x)}.\)

<tbc>Hence \(f'_w(x)=0\) if and only if \(x=m_j^\alpha(w)\). Also,

\(f''_w(x)=\frac{\alpha\mu_{i^\star}+w\mu_j}{x^2}+\frac{\alpha(1-\mu_{i^\star})+w(1-\mu_j)}{(1-x)^2}>0,\)

so _f<sub>w</sub>_ is strictly convex and the minimizer is unique.

Because \(w\mapsto m_j^\alpha(w)\) is smooth, so is \(I_j^\alpha\). The envelope theorem gives<tbc>

\(\frac{d}{dw}I_j^\alpha(w)=\frac{\partial}{\partial w}f_w(m_j^\alpha(w))=d(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w)).\)

<tbc>Since \(\mu_j<\mu_{i^\star}\), one has \(m_j^\alpha(w)\in(\mu_j,\mu_{i^\star})\), and therefore \(d(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w))>0\). Finally,<tbc>

\(\frac{d}{dq}d(p,q)=\frac{q-p}{q(1-q)},\frac{d}{dw}m_j^\alpha(w)=\frac{\alpha(\mu_j-\mu_{i^\star})}{(\alpha+w)^2}.\)

<tbc>Differentiating once more yields<tbc>

\(\frac{d^2}{dw^2}I_j^\alpha(w)=\frac{m_j^\alpha(w)-\mu_j}{m_j^\alpha(w)(1-m_j^\alpha(w))}\cdot\frac{\alpha(\mu_j-\mu_{i^\star})}{(\alpha+w)^2}.\)

<tbc>Using

\(m_j^\alpha(w)-\mu_j=\frac{\alpha(\mu_{i^\star}-\mu_j)}{\alpha+w},\)

we recover the stated formula, which is strictly negative.

## C.2 Boundary behavior and inverse maps

**Lemma C.2** (Boundary behavior)**.** _Fix_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) _and_ \(j\neq i^\star\)_. Then_

\(lim_{w\downarrow 0}I_j^\alpha(w)=0,lim_{w\uparrow\infty} I_j^\alpha(w)=\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},\mu_j).\)

_Consequently,_ \(I_j^\alpha\) _is a_ \(C^\infty\) _strictly increasing bijection from_ \((0,\infty)\) _onto_ \((0,\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},\mu_j))\).

_Proof of Lemma C.2._ By Proposition C.1,<tbc>

\(I_j^\alpha(w)=\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},m_j^\alpha(w))+wd(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w)).\)

<tbc>As \(w\downarrow 0\), \(m_j^\alpha(w)\rightarrow\mu_{i^\star}\), so both terms vanish. As \(w\uparrow\infty\), \(m_j^\alpha(w)\rightarrow\mu_j\), and hence<tbc>

\(\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},m_j^\alpha(w))\rightarrow\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},\mu_j).\)

<tbc>Moreover,

\(m_j^\alpha(w)-\mu_j=\frac{\alpha(\mu_{i^\star}-\mu_j)}{\alpha+w}=O(w^{-1}),\)

and _d(p,q_)=_O_((_q-p_)<sup>2</sup>) as \(q\rightarrow p\). Therefore \(wd(\mu_j,m_j^\alpha(w))\rightarrow 0\). The bijection claim follows from Proposition C.1 and the two endpoint limits.

**Proposition C.3** (Unique fixed-\(\alpha\) optimizer)**.** _For every_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) _there exist a unique vector_ \(w^\alpha(\mu)\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}\) _and a unique scalar_ \(\lambda_\alpha>0\) _such that_<tbc>

\(I_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha(\mu))=\lambda_\alpha\forall j\neq i^\star.\)

<tbc>_Moreover,_ \(\lambda_\alpha=T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\)_, and the map_

\(\alpha\longmapsto\big(w^\alpha(\mu),T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\big)\)

_is C_<sup>1</sup> _on compact subsets of_ (0,1).

_Proof of Proposition C.3._ Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and define<tbc>

\(\Delta_j:=d(\mu_{i^\star},\mu_j)>0,j\neq i^\star.\)

<tbc>By Lemma C.2, for each fixed \(\alpha\) the map \(I_j^\alpha:(0,\infty)\rightarrow(0,\alpha\Delta_j)\) is a strictly increasing \(C^\infty\) bijection. Define<tbc>

\(G_j(\alpha,\lambda):=(I_j^\alpha)^{-1}(\lambda),0<\lambda<\alpha\Delta_j.\)

<tbc>Let<tbc>

\(\Delta_\mathrm{min}:=\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i^\star}\Delta_j,F(\alpha,\lambda):=\sum_{j\neq i^\star} G_j(\alpha,\lambda)-(1-\alpha),\)

<tbc>on the domain<tbc>

\(\{(\alpha,\lambda):\alpha\in(0,1),0<\lambda<\alpha\Delta_\mathrm{min}\}.\)

<tbc>For fixed \(\alpha\), the map \(\lambda\mapsto F(\alpha,\lambda)\) is continuous and strictly increasing. In addition,

\(\mathrm{lim}_{\lambda\downarrow 0}F(\alpha,\lambda)=-(1-\alpha)<0,\)

whereas

\(\mathrm{lim}_{\lambda\uparrow\alpha\Delta_\mathrm{min}}F(\alpha,\lambda)=+\infty,\)

because at least one inverse diverges as \(\lambda\uparrow\alpha\Delta_\mathrm{min}\). Therefore there exists a unique \(\lambda_\alpha\in(0,\alpha\Delta_\mathrm{min})\) satisfying \(F(\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)=0\). Set \(w_j^\alpha(\mu):=G_j(\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)\). Then \(w^\alpha(\mu)\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}\) and \(I_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha(\mu))=\lambda_\alpha\) for every \(j\neq i^\star\).

For optimality, let \(w\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}\) and write<tbc>

\(m(w):=\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i^\star} I_j^\alpha(w_j).\)

<tbc>Since each \(I_j^\alpha\) is increasing,<tbc>

\(w_j\ge G_j(\alpha,m(w))\forall j\neq i^\star.\)

Summing over \(j\neq i^\star\) gives<tbc>

\(1-\alpha=\sum_{j\neq i^\star} w_j\ge\sum_{j\neq i^\star} G_j(\alpha,m(w)).\)

<tbc>By the defining property of \(\lambda_\alpha\), this implies \(m(w)\le\lambda_\alpha\). Hence

\(max_{w\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}}min_{j\neq i^\star} I_j^\alpha(w_j)=\lambda_\alpha,\)

and therefore \(\lambda_\alpha=T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\). If _w_ is any maximizer, then \(m(w)=\lambda_\alpha\), so \(w_j\ge G_j(\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)=w_j^\alpha(\mu)\) for every \(j\neq i^\star\). Because both vectors sum to \(1-\alpha\), equality must hold coordinatewise, proving uniqueness.

For regularity, define<tbc>

\(\Psi_j(\alpha,w,\lambda):=I_j^\alpha(w)-\lambda.\)

<tbc>Since \(\Psi_j\) is _C_<sup>1</sup> and \(\partial_w\Psi_j(\alpha,w,\lambda)=\partial_wI_j^\alpha(w)>0\), the inverse function theorem implies that _G<sub>j</sub>_ is _C_<sup>1</sup> on its domain. Hence _F_ is _C_<sup>1</sup>, with

\(\partial_\lambda F(\alpha,\lambda)=\sum_{j\neq i^\star}\partial_\lambda G_j(\alpha,\lambda)>0.\)

The implicit function theorem applied to \(F(\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)=0\) shows that \(\alpha\mapsto\lambda_\alpha\) is _C_<sup>1</sup> on compact subsets of (0,1). Each coordinate \(\alpha\mapsto w_j^\alpha(\mu)=G_j(\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)\) is therefore _C_<sup>1</sup> as well.

**Lemma C.4** (Lipschitz control of \(T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\) on compacts)**.** _Let_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\) _be compact. Then there exists a finite constant_ \(L_\mu(U)\) _such that for all_ \(\alpha,\alpha'\in U\),

\(\left|\frac{1}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}-\frac{1}{T_{\alpha^\prime}^\star(\mu)}\right|\le L_\mu(U)|\alpha-\alpha'|.\)

_Proof of Lemma C.4._ By Proposition C.3, the map \(\alpha\mapsto T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\) is _C_<sup>1</sup> on an open neighborhood of _U_. Its derivative is continuous and therefore bounded on the compact set _U_. The mean value theorem yields the displayed Lipschitz bound.

## C.3 Discrete rounding and proof of Proposition 4.1

**Lemma C.5** (Integer rounding with a fixed sum)**.** _Let_ \(a_1,\dots,a_{K-1}\ge 1\) _satisfy_ \(\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}a_j=s\in\mathbb{N}\)_. Then there exist integers_ \(m_1,\dots,m_{K-1}\ge 1\) _such that_

\(\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}m_j=s,|m_j-a_j|\le 1\forall j.\)

_Proof of Lemma C.5._ Let \(\widetilde{m}_j:=\lfloor a_j\rfloor\), so \(\widetilde{m}_j\ge 1\) for all _j_, and define \(r:=s-\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}\widetilde{m}_j\). Because \(\sum_ja_j=s\) and each fractional part satisfies \(a_j-\lfloor a_j\rfloor<1\), one has \(r\in\{0,1,\dots,K-2\}\). Add 1 to the _r_ coordinates with largest fractional parts. The resulting integers satisfy the required properties.

_Proof of Proposition 4.1._ Fix \(U\Subset(0,1)\). We show that there exists \(C_\mu(U)<\infty\) such that for every \(n\ge 1\) and \(s\ge K-1\) with<tbc>

\(\alpha:=\frac{n}{n+s}\in U,t:=n+s,\)

<tbc>one has<tbc>

\(\left|\Gamma_{n,s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)-\left(\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+\mathrm{log}t\right)\right|\le C_\mu(U).\)

<tbc>Let \(m=(m_j)_{j\neq i^\star}\) be any feasible integer allocation and define _w<sub>j</sub>_:=_m<sub>j</sub>/t_. Then \(w\in\Delta_{1-\alpha}\) and<tbc>

\(\Phi_j(n,m_j)=tI_j^\alpha(w_j)+\mathrm{log}t+\mathrm{log}w_j.\)

For the upper bound, note that 0_\<w<sub>j</sub>\<_1, hence \(\mathrm{log}w_j\le 0\). Therefore<tbc>

\(\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i^\star}\Phi_j(n,m_j)\le\mathrm{log}t+t\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i^\star} I_j^\alpha(w_j)\le\mathrm{log}t+\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}.\)

<tbc>Maximizing over feasible _m_ yields<tbc>

\(\Gamma_{n,s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)\le\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+\mathrm{log}t.\)

<tbc>For the lower bound, let \(w^\alpha(\mu)\) be the optimizer from Proposition C.3. Since \(\alpha\mapsto w^\alpha(\mu)\) is continuous on _U_ and all coordinates are positive,<tbc>

\(c_U:=\mathrm{inf}_{\alpha\in U}\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i^\star} w_j^\alpha(\mu)>0.\)

<tbc>Similarly,<tbc>

\(L_U:=\mathrm{sup}_{\alpha\in U}\mathrm{sup}_{j\neq i^\star}\mathrm{sup}_{u\in[c_U/2,1]}\left|\frac{d}{du}I_j^\alpha(u)\right|<\infty.\)

<tbc>Assume first that \(t\ge 2/c_U\). Then \(a_j:=tw_j^\alpha(\mu)\ge 2\), so Lemma C.5 gives integers \(m_j\ge 1\) such that<tbc>

\(\sum_{j\neq i^\star} m_j=s,|m_j-tw_j^\alpha(\mu)|\le 1.\)

<tbc>Hence<tbc>

\(\left|\frac{m_j}{t}-w_j^\alpha(\mu)\right|\le\frac{1}{t},\frac{m_j}{t}\ge\frac{c_U}{2}.\)

<tbc>By the mean value theorem,<tbc>

\(\left|I_j^\alpha\left(\frac{m_j}{t}\right)-I_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha(\mu))\right|\le\frac{L_U}{t}.\)

<tbc>Since \(I_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha(\mu))=T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\),<tbc>

\(tI_j^\alpha\left(\frac{m_j}{t}\right)\ge\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}-L_U.\)

<tbc>Moreover, \(\mathrm{log}(m_j/t)\ge\mathrm{log}(c_U/2)\). Therefore<tbc>

\(\Phi_j(n,m_j)\ge\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+\mathrm{log}t-L_U+\mathrm{log}(c_U/2)\forall j\neq i^\star.\)

<tbc>Taking the minimum over _j_ gives

\(\Gamma_{n,s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)\ge\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+\mathrm{log}t-C_{1,\mu}(U),\)

where \(C_{1,\mu}(U):=L_U-\mathrm{log}(c_U/2)\).

If _t\<_2_/c<sub>U</sub>_, only finitely many admissible triples (_n,s,t_) satisfy _n+s=t_ and \(n/(n+s)\in U\), so their contribution can be absorbed into a finite constant \(C_{0,\mu}(U)\). Taking \(C_\mu(U):=\mathrm{max}\{C_{0,\mu}(U),C_{1,\mu}(U)\}\) completes the proof.

## D Time-Uniform Pairwise GLR Control

### D.1 Armwise KL confidence sequences

**Lemma D.1** (Armwise KL confidence sequences)**.** _There exists a universal constant c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 _such that for every_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _there is an event_ \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\) _with_ \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{K}_\eta)\ge 1-\eta\) _and, on_ \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\)_, simultaneously for all_ \(t\ge K\) _and all arms_ \(i\in[K]\),<tbc>

\(N_{t,i}d(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i},\mu_i)\le c_0\left(\mathrm{log}\frac{K}{\eta}+\mathrm{loglog}(et)\right).\)

<tbc>_Consequently,_<tbc>

\(|\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}-\mu_i|\le\sqrt{\frac{c_0H_t(\eta)}{2N_{t,i}}}.\)

_Proof of Lemma D.1._ For each arm \(i\in[K]\), let \((Y_{i,s})_{s\ge 1}\) be the reward sequence of arm _i_, indexed by pull number. Since arm _i_ is Bernoulli\((\mu_i)\), the sequence \((Y_{i,s})_{s\ge 1}\) is i.i.d. Bernoulli\((\mu_i)\). For \(n\ge 1\), define

\(\overline{Y_{i,n}}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{s=1}^nY_{i,s}.\)

By construction,

\(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}=\overline{Y_{i,N_{t,i}}}\text{for all}t\ge K.\)

Since the algorithm pulls each arm once initially, \(N_{t,i}\ge 1\).

Apply the one-dimensional time-uniform KL confidence-sequence bound for one-parameter exponential families from Kaufmann and Koolen \[13, Section 3.3.2, Equation (14)\], specialized to Bernoulli distributions. There is a universal constant _c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 such that, for every \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), there exists an event \(\mathcal{E}_i(\gamma)\) with \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{E}_i(\gamma))\ge 1-\gamma\) and such that, on \(\mathcal{E}_i(\gamma)\), simultaneously for all \(n\ge 1\),

\(nd(\overline{Y_{i,n}},\mu_i)\le c_0\left(log\frac{1}{\gamma}+loglog(en)\right).\)

Choose \(\gamma=\eta/K\) and define \(\mathcal{K}_\eta:=\cap_{i=1}^K\mathcal{E}_i(\eta/K)\). A union bound gives \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{K}_\eta)\ge 1-\eta\).

Because the confidence-sequence bound is uniform over all \(n\ge 1\), we may evaluate it at the random sample size _n=N<sub>t,i</sub>_. On \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\), simultaneously for all \(t\ge K\) and all \(i\in[K]\),

\(N_{t,i}d(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i},\mu_i)\le c_0\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog(eN_{t,i})\right)\le c_0\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog(et)\right).\)

Pinsker’s inequality, \(d(p,q)\ge 2(p-q)^2\), yields the displayed radius bound.

## D.2 Local Lipschitz control of the Bernoulli GLR

**Lemma D.2** (Bregman representation and local Lipschitz control)**.** _Fix_ \(m,\ell\ge 1\) _and_ \(p,q\in(0,1)\)_. Let_<tbc>

\(\alpha:=\frac{m}{m+\ell},F(x):=xlogx+(1-x)log(1-x),\)

<tbc>_with the continuous extension to_ \[0,1\]_. Then_<tbc>

\(V_{m,\ell}(p,q)=(m+\ell)\left[\alpha F(p)+(1-\alpha)F(q)-F(\alpha p+(1-\alpha)q)\right],\)

<tbc>_where_<tbc>

\(V_{m,\ell}(p,q):=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{md(p,x)+\ell d(q,x)\right\}.\)

<tbc>_Moreover, for every_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) _and all_ \(p,q,u,v\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\),<tbc>

\(|V_{m,\ell}(p,q)-V_{m,\ell}(u,v)|\le\frac{2}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}\frac{m\ell}{m+\ell}\left(|p-u|+|q-v|\right).\)

<tbc>_Proof of Lemma D.2._ The minimizer in the definition of \(V_{m,\ell}(p,q)\) is \(r=\alpha p+(1-\alpha)q\). Substitution gives the Bregman representation.

For the Lipschitz bound, write<tbc>

\(V_{m,\ell}(p,q)=(m+\ell)\left[\alpha F(p)+(1-\alpha)F(q)-F(r)\right],r=\alpha p+(1-\alpha)q.\)

<tbc>Then<tbc>

\(\partial_pV_{m,\ell}(p,q)=m(F'(p)-F'(r)),\partial_qV_{m,\ell}(p,q)=\ell(F'(q)-F'(r)).\)

<tbc>Since \(F''(x)=1/[x(1-x)]\), on \([\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\) one has<tbc>

\(|F'(x)-F'(y)|\le\frac{|x-y|}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}.\)

<tbc>Moreover,<tbc>

\(|p-r|=(1-\alpha)|p-q|\le 1-\alpha,|q-r|=\alpha|p-q|\le\alpha.\)

<tbc>Thus

\(|\partial_pV_{m,\ell}(p,q)|\le\frac{m(1-\alpha)}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}=\frac{m\ell}{m+\ell}\frac{1}{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)},\)

and the same bound holds for \(|\partial_qV_{m,\ell}(p,q)|\). Applying the mean value theorem first in the _p_ coordinate and then in the _q_ coordinate proves the displayed inequality. The factor 2 is a harmless slack that keeps the bound uniform over the two coordinate changes.

### D.3 Proof of Theorem 4.2

_Proof of Theorem 4.2._ Work on the armwise confidence event \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\) from Lemma D.1. This event has probability at least \(1-\eta\). Fix \(t\ge K\) and \(i\neq j\), and set<tbc>

\(m=N_{t,i},\ell=N_{t,j},H=H_t(\eta),N_\mathrm{eff}=\frac{m\ell}{m+\ell}.\)

<tbc>On \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\),<tbc>

\(|\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}-\mu_i|\le\sqrt{\frac{c_0H}{2m}},|\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}-\mu_j|\le\sqrt{\frac{c_0H}{2\ell}}.\)

<tbc>Let<tbc>

\(\varepsilon_\mu=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{min}_{a\in[K]}\{\mu_a,1-\mu_a\}.\)

<tbc>First suppose that<tbc>

\(\mathrm{min}\{m,\ell\}\le\frac{2c_0}{\varepsilon_\mu^2}H.\)

<tbc>Assume without loss of generality that \(m\le\ell\). Evaluating the empirical infimum defining _V<sub>t</sub>(i,j_) at \(x=\mu_j\) gives<tbc>

\(V_t(i,j)\le md(\widehat{\mu}_{t,i},\mu_j)+\ell d(\widehat{\mu}_{t,j},\mu_j).\)

<tbc>The first term is at most \(C_\mu m\) because \(p\mapsto d(p,\mu_j)\) is bounded on \[0,1\], and the second term is at most _c_<sub>0</sub>_H_ on \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\). Thus \(V_t(i,j)\le C_\mu H\). The same evaluation at \(x=\mu_j\) gives<tbc>

\(V_t^\mu(i,j)\le md(\mu_i,\mu_j)\le C_\mu m\le C_\mu H.\)

<tbc>Hence<tbc>

\(|V_t(i,j)-V_t^\mu(i,j)|\le C_\mu H\)

<tbc>in the small-count regime.

<tbc>Now suppose that<tbc>

\(\mathrm{min}\{m,\ell\}>\frac{2c_0}{\varepsilon_\mu^2}H.\)

<tbc>Then both empirical means belong to \([\varepsilon_\mu/2,1-\varepsilon_\mu/2]\), and all true means belong to the same interval. Lemma D.2, applied with \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_\mu/2\), gives<tbc>

\(|V_t(i,j)-V_t^\mu(i,j)|\le C_\mu N_\mathrm{eff}\left(|\widehat{\mu}_{t,i}-\mu_i|+|\widehat{\mu}_{t,j}-\mu_j|\right).\)

<tbc>Using the armwise confidence radii,<tbc>

\(|V_t(i,j)-V_t^\mu(i,j)|\le C_\mu N_\mathrm{eff}\left(\sqrt{\frac{H}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{H}{\ell}}\right).\)

<tbc>Since \(N_\mathrm{eff}\le m\) and \(N_\mathrm{eff}\le\ell\),<tbc>

\(\frac{N_\mathrm{eff}}{\sqrt{m}}\le\sqrt{N_\mathrm{eff}},\frac{N_\mathrm{eff}}{\sqrt{\ell}}\le\sqrt{N_\mathrm{eff}}.\)

<tbc>Therefore,

\(|V_t(i,j)-V_t^\mu(i,j)|\le C_\mu\sqrt{N_\mathrm{eff}H}\)

in the large-count regime. Combining the two regimes proves the displayed bound. The event \(\mathcal{K}_\eta\) is simultaneous over all arms and all sample sizes, so the conclusion holds simultaneously over all \(t\ge K\) and all pairs \(i\neq j\).

## E Evidence Bounds in the Stabilized Regime

Let \(G_{t+1}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the exploration guard is used at time _t_+1; for the unguarded rule, \(G_{t+1}\equiv 0\). We write<tbc>

\(\mathcal{J}:=[K]\backslash\{i^\star\},d_K:=|\mathcal{J}|=K-1.\)

<tbc>For \(j\in\mathcal{J}\), extend<tbc>

\(\Phi_j(n,m):=\mathrm{inf}_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{nd(\mu_{i^\star},x)+md(\mu_j,x)\right\}+\mathrm{log}m\)

<tbc>to real _m\>_0. For integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\ge d_K\),<tbc>

\(\Gamma_{n,S}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)=\mathrm{max}_{m_j\in\{1,2,\dots\}:\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}m_j=S}\mathrm{min}_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Phi_j(n,m_j).\)

## E.1 Continuous equalizers and slope bounds **Lemma E.1** (Uniform slope bounds for \(\Phi_j\))**.** _Fix a compact interval_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\)_. There exist constants_ \(0 \(c_\mu(U)\le\partial_m\Phi_j(n,m)\le C_\mu(U).\) _Proof of Lemma E.1._ By the envelope theorem, \(\partial_m\Phi_j(n,m)=d(\mu_j,x_j(n,m))+\frac{1}{m},x_j(n,m):=\frac{n\mu_{i^\star}+m\mu_j}{n+m}.\) If _aU_:=inf_U_, then for \(1\le m\le S+1\), \(\frac{n}{n+m}\ge\frac{n}{n+S+1}=\frac{\alpha(n+S)}{n+S+1}\ge\frac{a_U}{2}\) after enlarging constants for finitely many small values of _n+S_. Hence _xj(n,m_) stays uniformly separated from \(\mu_j\). Since \(\mu_{i^\star}>\mu_j\), the term \(d(\mu_j,x_j(n,m))\) has a positive lower bound depending only on \((\mu,U)\). The upper bound follows from \(x_j(n,m)\in[\mu_j,\mu_{i^\star}]\) and \(1/m\le 1\). **Lemma E.2** (Continuous equalizer and small-budget cutoff)**.** _Fix_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\)_. For each_ \(n\ge 1\)_, define_ \(\gamma_{min}(n):=max_{k\in\mathcal{J}}\Phi_k(n,1),S_0(n,\mu):=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma_{min}(n)),\) _where_ \(\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma)\) _is the inverse of_ \(m\mapsto\Phi_j(n,m)\) _on_ \([1,\infty)\)_. There exists_ \(\overline{S_\mu}<\infty\) _such that_ \(S_0(n,\mu)\le\overline{S_\mu}\) _for all_ \(n\ge 1\)_. For every_ \(S\ge S_0(n,\mu)\)_, there is a unique pair_ \((\gamma_{n,S},r_{n,S})\), \(r_{n,S}=(r_{j,n,S})_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\)_, satisfying_ \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}r_{j,n,S}=S,r_{j,n,S}\ge 1,\Phi_j(n,r_{j,n,S})=\gamma_{n,S}\forall j\in\mathcal{J}.\) _Moreover, if t=n+S,_ \(\alpha=n/t\in U\)_, and_ \(S\ge S_0(n,\mu)\)_, then_ \(\gamma_{n,S}=\frac{t}{T_\alpha^\star(\mu)}+logt+O_\mu(1),r_{j,n,S}=tw_j^\alpha(\mu)+O_\mu(1),\) _uniformly over_ \(\alpha\in U\)_, S, and_ \(j\in\mathcal{J}\)_. If S is an integer, then_ \(|\gamma_{n,S}-\Gamma_{n,S}^\text{disc}(\mu)|\le C_\mu(U).\) _Proof of Lemma E.2._ For fixed _n_, the map \(m\mapsto\Phi_j(n,m)\) is continuous on \((0,\infty)\) and strictly increasing. Indeed, \(\partial_m\Phi_j(n,m)=d(\mu_j,x_j(n,m))+\frac{1}{m}>0,x_j(n,m)=\frac{n\mu_{i^\star}+m\mu_j}{n+m}.\) Moreover \(\Phi_j(n,m)\rightarrow+\infty\) as \(m\rightarrow\infty\) because \(logm\rightarrow+\infty\). Thus the inverse on \([1,\infty)\) is well defined for every \(\gamma\ge\Phi_j(n,1)\).
Let \(D_\mu^{max}:=max_{k\in\mathcal{J}}d(\mu_k,\mu_{i^\star}).\) Evaluating \(\Phi_k(n,1)\) at \(x=\mu_{i^\star}\) gives \(\gamma_{min}(n)\le D_\mu^{max}\). Since \(\Phi_j(n,m)\ge logm\), any \(m\ge exp(D_\mu^{max})\) satisfies \(\Phi_j(n,m)\ge\gamma_{min}(n)\). Hence \(\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma_{min}(n))\le exp(D_\mu^{max}),S_0(n,\mu)\le\overline{S_\mu}:=d_Kexp(D_\mu^{max}).\) For \(S\ge S_0(n,\mu)\), define \(F_n(\gamma):=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma),\gamma\ge\gamma_{min}(n).\) Then _Fn_ is continuous and strictly increasing, \(F_n(\gamma_{min}(n))=S_0(n,\mu)\), and \(F_n(\gamma)\rightarrow\infty\) as \(\gamma\rightarrow\infty\). Therefore \(F_n(\gamma)=S\) has a unique solution \(\gamma_{n,S}\), and the corresponding coordinates

\(r_{j,n,S}:=\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma_{n,S})\) give the equalizer. This equalizer maximizes the real-valued max-min problem: if \(\gamma\) is feasible, then each coordinate must satisfy \(m_j\ge\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma)\), so feasibility requires \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Phi_j^{-1}(n,\gamma)\le S\); the largest such \(\gamma\) is exactly \(\gamma_{n,S}\).

Let \(\lambda_\alpha=T_\alpha^\star(\mu)^{-1}\) and let \(w^\alpha\) be the unique continuous optimizer from Proposition C.3. Writing _q<sub>j</sub>=r<sub>j,n,S</sub>/t_, the equalizer identity gives<tbc>

\(\gamma_{n,S}=tI_j^\alpha(q_j)+\mathrm{log}t+\mathrm{log}q_j\forall j\in\mathcal{J}.\)

<tbc>For the upper bound, choose _j_ minimizing \(I_j^\alpha(q_j)\). Since \(\sum_jq_j=1-\alpha\), Proposition C.3 gives \(\mathrm{min}_jI_j^\alpha(q_j)\le\lambda_\alpha\), and \(\mathrm{log}q_j\le 0\). Hence \(\gamma_{n,S}\le t\lambda_\alpha+\mathrm{log}t\). For the lower bound, use the real feasible allocation \(m_j=tw_j^\alpha\). Because \(\mathrm{inf}_{\alpha\in U,j}w_j^\alpha>0\), all these coordinates are at least one for all large _t_, and the finitely many remaining cases are absorbed into the constant. Thus

\(\gamma_{n,S}\ge\mathrm{min}_j\left\{tI_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha)+\mathrm{log}t+\mathrm{log}w_j^\alpha\right\}\ge t\lambda_\alpha+\mathrm{log}t-C_\mu(U).\)

This proves the estimate for \(\gamma_{n,S}\).

We next control _r<sub>j,n,S</sub>_. Let \(c_U:=\mathrm{inf}_{\alpha\in U,j}w_j^\alpha>0\). If _q<sub>j</sub>\<c<sub>U</sub>/_2, then uniformly in \(\alpha\in U\) the strict monotonicity of \(I_j^\alpha\) gives \(I_j^\alpha(q_j)\le\lambda_\alpha-\rho_U\) for some \(\rho_U>0\). For large _t_, this contradicts the lower bound on \(\gamma_{n,S}\); the finitely many small values of _t_ are absorbed into constants. Hence \(q_j\ge c_U/2\). Since log_q<sub>j</sub>=O<sub>U</sub>_(1), the equalizer identity and the estimate for \(\gamma_{n,S}\) imply

\(I_j^\alpha(q_j)=\lambda_\alpha+O_\mu(1/t).\)

On \[_c<sub>U</sub>/_2,1\], the derivative \(\partial_wI_j^\alpha(w)\) is uniformly bounded away from zero. The mean value theorem yields \(|q_j-w_j^\alpha|\le C_\mu(U)/t\), which is the asserted estimate for _r<sub>j,n,S</sub>_.

Finally assume _S_ is an integer. The continuous equalizer maximizes the real-valued max-min problem, so \(\Gamma_{n,S}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)\le\gamma_{n,S}\). Conversely, Lemma C.5 rounds _r<sub>n,S</sub>_ to integers \(\overline{r_j}\ge 1\) with \(\sum_j\overline{r_j}=S\) and \(|\overline{r_j}-r_{j,n,S}|\le 1\). Lemma E.1 gives \(\Phi_j(n,\overline{r_j})\ge\gamma_{n,S}-C_\mu(U)\), and hence \(\Gamma_{n,S}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)\ge\gamma_{n,S}-C_\mu(U)\).

## E.2 Guard-count control

**Lemma E.3** (Deterministic bound on the number of guard activations)**.** _Assume the guard rule is the following: at time t_+1_, if_ \(\mathrm{min}_iN_{t,i}<\sqrt{t/K}\)_, then the algorithm sets G_<sub>_t_+1</sub>=1 _and pulls a least-sampled arm. Then for all_ \(t\ge K\),<tbc>

\(G_t^\mathrm{tot}:=\sum_{u=K}^{t-1}G_{u+1}\le K\left(1+\left\lfloor\sqrt{t/K}\right\rfloor\right)\le\sqrt{K}t+K.\)

<tbc>_Proof of Lemma E.3._ For \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), define

\(\mathcal{I}_r:=\left\{u\ge K:r\le\sqrt{u/K}<r+1\right\}.\)

Fix _r_. If _G_<sub>_u_+1</sub>=1 for some \(u\in\mathcal{I}_r\), then a least-sampled arm has count at most _r_. After at most _K_ guard pulls inside I_<sub>r</sub>_, every arm has count at least _r_+1, and then the guard condition cannot hold again within the same epoch. There are at most \(1+\left\lfloor\sqrt{t/K}\right\rfloor\) epochs up to time _t_, which proves the claim.

## E.3 The uniform challenger-index lower bound

Let \(U\in(0,1)\) contain \(\beta\), and let _t<sub>U</sub>_ be a _U_-stabilization time:<tbc>

\(B_{t+1}=i^\star,\alpha_t:=\frac{N_{t,i^\star}}{t}\in U,\forall t\ge t_U.\)

<tbc>For \(s\ge t_U\), define<tbc>

\(n_s:=N_{s,i^\star},S_s:=s-n_s,m_{s,j}:=N_{s,j},j\in\mathcal{J}.\)

Thus \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}m_{s,j}=S_s\) and \(Q_s(j)=\Phi_j(n_s,m_{s,j})\). Let \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\) be the event from Theorem 4.2. On this event, simultaneously for all \(t\ge K\) and all \(j\in\mathcal{J}\),<tbc>

\(|P_t(j)-Q_t(j)|=|V_t(i^\star,j)-V_t^\mu(i^\star,j)|\le\varepsilon_t,\)

<tbc>where<tbc>

\(P_t(j)=V_t(i^\star,j)+logN_{t,j},Q_t(j)=V_t^\mu(i^\star,j)+logN_{t,j},\)

<tbc>and

\(\varepsilon_t:=C_\mu\left(\sqrt{tH_t(\eta)}+H_t(\eta)\right).\)

<tbc>**Lemma E.4** (Challenger-budget uniform lower bound)**.** _Fix_ \(U\Subset(0,1)\) _containing_ \(\beta\)_. There exists a finite constant_ \(C_\mu(U)<\infty\) _such that, on_ \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\)_, for every U-stabilization time t<sub>U</sub> and every_ \(s\ge t_U\),

\(min_{j\in\mathcal{J}}Q_s(j)\ge\Gamma_{n_s,S_s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+G_s^\mathrm{tot}+\varepsilon_s+\mathrm{sup}_{t_U\le u\le s}u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1\right).\) (E.1)

_For the unguarded rule,_ \(G_s^\mathrm{tot}\equiv 0\).

_Proof of Lemma E.4._ Let \(\overline{S_\mu}\) be the uniform cutoff from Lemma E.2 and set

\(\overline{\alpha_U}:=\mathrm{sup}U<1,s_\mathrm{eq}:=\left[\frac{\overline{S_\mu}}{1-\overline{\alpha_U}}\right].\)

If \(u\ge s_\mathrm{eq}\) and \(\alpha_u\in U\), then \(S_u=(1-\alpha_u)u\ge\overline{S_\mu}\), so the continuous equalizer \((\gamma_{n_u,S_u},r_{n_u,S_u})\) exists. If _s\<s_<sub>eq</sub>, only finitely many count configurations are possible; after enlarging \(C_\mu(U)\), the displayed bound is automatic because the factor in parentheses is at least one. We therefore assume \(s\ge s_\bullet:=\mathrm{max}\{t_U,s_\mathrm{eq}\}\). Then the equalizer exists for every \(u\in[s_\bullet,s]\).

Define the fixed-\(\beta\) challenger target<tbc>

\(p_j^\beta:=\frac{w_j^\beta}{1-\beta},j\in\mathcal{J},\)

<tbc>so that \(p_j^\beta>0\) and \(\sum_jp_j^\beta=1\). For \(u\in[s_\bullet,s]\), set<tbc>

\(D_{u,j}:=p_j^\beta S_u-N_{u,j},j\in\mathcal{J}.\)

<tbc>Then \(\sum_jD_{u,j}=0\). Lemma E.2 and the identity \(S_u=(1-\alpha_u)u\) give<tbc>

\(r_{j,n_u,S_u}-p_j^\beta S_u=u\left(w_j^{\alpha_u}-\frac{1-\alpha_u}{1-\beta}w_j^\beta\right)+O_\mu(1).\)

<tbc>The map<tbc>

\(\alpha\mapsto w_j^\alpha-\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\beta}w_j^\beta\)

<tbc>is _C_<sup>1</sup> on _U_ and vanishes at \(\alpha=\beta\). Hence, uniformly over \(u\in[s_\bullet,s]\),

\(|r_{j,n_u,S_u}-p_j^\beta S_u|\le C_\mu(U)(u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1).\) (E.2)

We next show that regular challenger pulls serve an approximately largest deficit. Let \(u+1\le s\) be a non-guard challenger-pull round with \(u\ge s_\bullet\), and let _a=C_<sub>_u_+1</sub>. Put \(M_u:=\mathrm{max}_{j\in\mathcal{J}}D_{u,j}\). We claim that, for constants \(\kappa_\mu(U)\in(0,1]\) and \(A_\mu(U)<\infty\),

\(D_{u,a}\ge\kappa_\mu(U)M_u-A_\mu(U)(\varepsilon_u+u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1).\) (E.3)

Let \(j^+\in\mathrm{argmax}_jD_{u,j}\) and define _e<sub>u,j</sub>_:=_r<sub>j,n<sub>u</sub>,S<sub>u</sub></sub>-N<sub>u,j</sub>_. By (E.2),

\(e_{u,j^+}\ge M_u-C_\mu(U)(u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1).\) (E.4)

If \(M_u\le C_\mu(U)(\varepsilon_u+u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1)\), then (E.3) follows after increasing \(A_\mu(U)\), because the zero-sum property implies \(D_{u,a}\ge-d_KM_u\). Otherwise _e_<sub>_u,j_<sup>+</sup></sub>_\>_0, and the slope lower bound in Lemma E.1 gives<tbc>

\(Q_u(j^+)\le\gamma_{n_u,S_u}-c_\mu(U)M_u+C_\mu(U)(u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1).\)

Since _a_ minimizes _P<sub>u</sub>_ and \(|P_u(j)-Q_u(j)|\le\varepsilon_u\) on \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\),<tbc>

\(Q_u(a)\le Q_u(j^+)+2\varepsilon_u.\)

<tbc>Thus \(\gamma_{n_u,S_u}-Q_u(a)\) is bounded below by \(c_\mu(U)M_u-C_\mu(U)(\varepsilon_u+u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1)\). In the present case this lower bound is positive, so _e<sub>u,a</sub>\>_0, and the slope upper bound yields

\(e_{u,a}\ge c'_\mu(U)M_u-C'_\mu(U)(\varepsilon_u+u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1).\)

Combining this with (E.2) proves (E.3).

Define \(P_u^+:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}(D_{u,j})_+\). Since the deficits sum to zero, \(M_u\le P_u^+\). Fix the final time _s_ and set<tbc>

\(\Xi_s:=\varepsilon_s+sup_{t_U\le v\le s}v|\alpha_v-\beta|+1,\Lambda_s:=\frac{A_\mu(U)\Xi_s+1}{\kappa_\mu(U)}.\)

<tbc>The sequence \(\varepsilon_u\) is nondecreasing, so (E.3) implies that every regular challenger pull \(u+1\le s\) with \(u\ge s_\bullet\) satisfies<tbc>

\(D_{u,C_{u+1}}\ge\kappa_\mu(U)M_u-A_\mu(U)\Xi_s.\)

<tbc>If _u_+1 is a leader pull, then _D_<sub>_u_+1</sub>=_D<sub>u</sub>_. If it is a challenger pull of arm _a_, then<tbc>

\(D_{u+1,j}=D_{u,j}+p_j^\beta-\mathbf{1}\{j=a\}.\)

<tbc>Consider a regular challenger pull. If \(M_u>\Lambda_s\), then _D<sub>u,a</sub>\>_1. Adding \(p^\beta\) can increase _P_<sup>+</sup> by at most \(\sum_jp_j^\beta=1\), while subtracting one from coordinate _a_ decreases the positive mass by exactly one. Hence \(P_{u+1}^+\le P_u^+\). If \(M_u\le\Lambda_s\), then \(P_u^+\le d_K\Lambda_s\), and a single challenger update can increase _P_<sup>+</sup> by at most one. Therefore every regular challenger pull satisfies

\(P_{u+1}^+\le max\{P_u^+,d_K\Lambda_s+1\}.\)

A guard pull is adversarial: if it pulls _i<sup>⋆</sup>_, _D_ is unchanged, and if it pulls a challenger, the same update holds for an arbitrary arm, increasing _P_<sup>+</sup> by at most one.

Induction from \(s_\bullet\) to _s_ gives<tbc>

\(P_s^+\le max\{P_{s_\bullet}^+,d_K\Lambda_s+1\}+G_s^\mathrm{tot}.\)

<tbc>Moreover,<tbc>

\(P_{s_\bullet}^+\le\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}p_j^\beta S_{s_\bullet}=S_{s_\bullet}\le s_\bullet\le t_U+s_\mathrm{eq},\)

<tbc>and _s_<sub>eq</sub> is absorbed into the constant. Hence<tbc>

\(P_s^+\le C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+G_s^\mathrm{tot}+\varepsilon_s+sup_{t_U\le u\le s}u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1\right).\)

<tbc>By (E.2), this implies<tbc>

\(max_{j\in\mathcal{J}}(r_{j,n_s,S_s}-N_{s,j})_+\le C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+G_s^\mathrm{tot}+\varepsilon_s+sup_{t_U\le u\le s}u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1\right).\)

<tbc>Let the right-hand side be _E<sub>s</sub>_. Then \(N_{s,j}\ge r_{j,n_s,S_s}-E_s\) for all _j_. If \(N_{s,j}\ge r_{j,n_s,S_s}\), monotonicity gives \(Q_s(j)\ge\gamma_{n_s,S_s}\). Otherwise Lemma E.1 gives \(Q_s(j)\ge\gamma_{n_s,S_s}-C_\mu(U)E_s\). Thus

\(min_{j\in\mathcal{J}}Q_s(j)\ge\gamma_{n_s,S_s}-C_\mu(U)E_s.\)

Using \(\gamma_{n_s,S_s}\ge\Gamma_{n_s,S_s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)-C_\mu(U)\) from Lemma E.2 proves the lemma.

## E.4 Proof of Proposition 5.1

_Proof of Proposition 5.1._ Write<tbc>

\(\widetilde{H}_s(\eta):=\mathrm{log}\frac{K}{\eta}+\mathrm{log}(es).\)

Let \(\mathcal{A}_\eta\) be the event from Proposition F.1. Define<tbc>

\(\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{env}(\eta):=\mathcal{G}_\eta\cap\mathcal{A}_\eta.\)

<tbc>By Theorem 4.2 and Proposition F.1, this event has probability at least \(1-2\eta\). On \(\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{env}(\eta)\), Lemma E.4 gives, for every \(s\ge t_U\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{min}_{j\in\mathcal{J}}Q_s(j)\ge\Gamma_{n_s,S_s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+G_s^\mathrm{tot}+\varepsilon_s+\mathrm{sup}_{t_U\le u\le s}u|\alpha_u-\beta|+1\right).\)

\(u|\alpha_u-\beta|\le C_\beta t_U+C_\beta\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+G_s^\mathrm{tot}.\)

\(\varepsilon_s\le C_\mu\left(\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right),\)

the first displayed inequality in Proposition 5.1 follows.

For the empirical transportation costs, on \(\mathcal{G}_\eta\),<tbc>

\(|P_s(j)-Q_s(j)|\le C_\mu\left(\sqrt{sH_s(\eta)}+H_s(\eta)\right)\le C_\mu\left(\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right).\)

\(\mathrm{min}_jP_s(j)\ge\mathrm{min}_jQ_s(j)-C_\mu\left(\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right).\)

\(W_s(i^\star,j)=P_s(j)-\mathrm{log}N_{s,j}\ge P_s(j)-\mathrm{log}s.\)

<tbc>Combining this with Proposition 4.1,

\(\Gamma_{n_s,S_s}^\mathrm{disc}(\mu)\ge\frac{s}{T_{\alpha_s}^\star(\mu)}+\mathrm{log}s-C_\mu(U),\)

## E.5 Challenger growth and separation

_Proof of Proposition 5.3._ Fix \(s\ge t_U\) and \(j\neq i^\star\). Proposition 5.1 gives<tbc>

\(Q_s(j)\ge\frac{s}{T_{\alpha_s}^\star(\mu)}-C_\mu(U)\left(t_U+\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}+\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\right)-\overline{C_\mu}(U).\)

<tbc>Since \(\alpha_s\in U\), the leading term is at least \(\lambda_{\mu,U}s\). On the other hand, evaluating the population transportation cost at \(x=\mu_{i^\star}\) yields

\(Q_s(j)=V_s^\mu(i^\star,j)+\mathrm{log}N_{s,j}\le d(\mu_j,\mu_{i^\star})N_{s,j}+\mathrm{log}s.\)

Combining the two inequalities gives the claim.

**Lemma E.5** (Logarithmic separation thresholds)**.** _There exists_ \(A_\mu<\infty\) _such that for all_ \(\eta\in(0,1/2]\),<tbc>

\(n_\star(\eta)\le A_\mu\left(\mathrm{log}\frac{K}{\eta}+\mathrm{loglog}\frac{e}{\eta}+1\right).\)

<tbc>_Proof of Lemma E.5._ For each \(j\neq i^\star\), let \(\Delta_j:=\mu_{i^\star}-\mu_j>0\). The condition defining \(n_j(\eta)\) is<tbc>

\(\frac{c_0}{2n}\left(\mathrm{log}\frac{8K^2}{\eta}+\mathrm{loglog}(en)\right)\le\frac{\Delta_j^2}{16}.\)

\(n\ge A\left(log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog\frac{e}{\eta}+1\right)\)

with _A_ sufficiently large implies the previous display uniformly over \(\eta\in(0,1/2]\). This follows from \(loglog(en)\le C_A+\frac{1}{2}log(e/\eta)\) after increasing _A_, and from the linear dominance of _n_ over the logarithmic terms. Taking the maximum over the finite set \(j\neq i^\star\) proves the claim.

_Proof of Corollary 5.4._ Let

\(L_\eta:=log\frac{K}{\eta}+loglog\frac{e}{\eta}+1.\)

By Lemma E.5, \(n_\star(\eta)\le A_\mu L_\eta\). Choose<tbc>

\(s=\left\lceil C_{\mu,\beta,U}(t_U+L_\eta)\right\rceil,\)

<tbc>with the constant to be fixed. For any \(\rho>0\), the elementary inequalities \(\sqrt{s\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)}\le\rho s+C_\rho\widetilde{H}_s(\eta)\) and \(log(es)\le\rho s+C_\rho\) imply<tbc>

## F Leader-Fraction Control and Threshold Inversion

### F.1 Uniform leader-fraction concentration

**Proposition F.1** (Leader-fraction control, uniform in the start time)**.** _There exists a constant_ \(c_\beta>0\) _such that for every_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _there exists an event_ \(\mathcal{A}_\eta\) _with_ \(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{A}_\eta)\ge 1-\eta\) _on which the following holds. For all integers_ \(m\ge 1\) _and all_ \(t\ge m\)_, if B_<sub>_u_+1</sub>=_i<sup>⋆</sup> for all_ \(u\ge m\)_, then_<tbc>

\(|(N_{t,i^\star}-N_{m,i^\star})-\beta(t-m)|\le c_\beta\sqrt{(t-m+1)log\left(\frac{etm^2}{\eta}\right)}+G_t^\text{tot}(m),\)

<tbc>_where_ \(G_t^\text{tot}(m):=\sum_{u=m}^{t-1}G_{u+1}\) _is the number of guard activations in_ {_m_+1_,...,t}. Consequently,_

\(|\alpha_t-\beta|\le\frac{(1+\beta)m}{t}+c_\beta\sqrt{\frac{1}{t}log\left(\frac{etm^2}{\eta}\right)}+\frac{G_t^\text{tot}(m)}{t}.\)

_Proof of Proposition F.1._ Fix \(\eta\in(0,1)\). For each \(m\ge 1\), set \(\eta_m:=6\eta/(\pi^2m^2)\) so that \(\sum_{m\ge 1}\eta_m\le\eta\).

Fix \(m\ge 1\) and assume _B_<sub>_u_+1</sub>=_i<sup>⋆</sup>_ for all \(u\ge m\). For the analysis, we enlarge the probability space by drawing an independent \(U_{u+1}\sim Ber(\beta)\) at every round, including guard rounds where this variable is not used by the algorithm. This does not change the law of the algorithm.

Fix \(m\ge 1\). For \(u\ge m\), define<tbc>

\(Z_{u+1}^{(m)}:=(U_{u+1}-\beta)\mathbf{1}\{G_{u+1}=0\}.\)

<tbc>Since _G_<sub>_u_+1</sub> is F_<sub>u</sub>_-measurable and _U_<sub>_u_+1</sub> is independent of F_<sub>u</sub>_ with mean \(\beta\), one has<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{u+1}^{(m)}|\mathcal{F}_u\right]=0,|Z_{u+1}^{(m)}|\le 1.\)

## F.3 Centered quantile integration

**Theorem F.3** (Centered quantile integration)**.** _Let_ \(X\ge 0\) _be a random variable. Let_ \(A\ge 0\) _and let_ \(r:(0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty)\) _satisfy_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}(X\le A+r(\eta))\ge 1-\eta\forall\eta\in(0,1].\)

<tbc>_Define the monotone envelope_<tbc>

\(r^\downarrow(\eta):=sup_{\xi\in[\eta,1]}r(\xi).\)

<tbc>_Then_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\le A+\int_0^1r^\downarrow(u)du.\)

<tbc>_Moreover, if_<tbc>

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}r^\downarrow(2^{-k})<\infty,\)

<tbc>_then_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\le A+\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}r^\downarrow(2^{-k}).\)

<tbc>_Proof of Theorem F.3._ Let<tbc>

\(Q_X(u):=inf\{x\ge 0:\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\ge 1-u\},u\in(0,1],\)

<tbc>be the upper-tail quantile of _X_. The assumed upper-quantile inequality gives<tbc>

\(Q_X(u)\le A+r(u)\le A+r^\downarrow(u)\forall u\in(0,1].\)

<tbc>The quantile representation of expectation for nonnegative random variables therefore yields<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^1Q_X(u)du\le A+\int_0^1r^\downarrow(u)du.\)

<tbc>For the dyadic bound, note that \(r^\downarrow\) is nonincreasing as a function of \(\eta\). Hence, for \(u\in[2^{-k-1},2^{-k}]\),<tbc>

\(r^\downarrow(u)\le r^\downarrow(2^{-k-1}).\)

<tbc>Consequently,

\(\int_0^1r^\downarrow(u)du\le\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k-1}r^\downarrow(2^{-k-1})\le\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}r^\downarrow(2^{-k}).\)

Combining this estimate with the first part proves the theorem.

**Lemma F.4** (Monotone summable upper-quantile bound)**.** _Let_ \(T\ge 0\) _be a random time. Suppose that T admits a summable upper-quantile bound function u<sub>T</sub>, namely_ \(\mathbb{P}(T\le u_T(\eta))\ge 1-\eta,\forall\eta\in(0,1]\)_, and_ \(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}u_T(2^{-k})<\infty\)_. Define the upper-tail quantile_

\(q_T(\eta):=inf\{x\ge 0:\mathbb{P}(T\le x)\ge 1-\eta\},\eta\in(0,1].\)

_Then q<sub>T</sub> is a nonincreasing upper-quantile bound for T, and_ \(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_T(2^{-k})<\infty\)_. Consequently, whenever a random time admits a summable upper-quantile bound, it admits a nonincreasing summable upper-quantile bound._

_Proof of Lemma F.4._ By definition of _q<sub>T</sub>_, one has<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}(T\le q_T(\eta))\ge 1-\eta\forall\eta\in(0,1].\)

<tbc>Thus _q<sub>T</sub>_ is a upper-quantile bound. If \(\eta_1\le\eta_2\), then \(1-\eta_1\ge 1-\eta_2\), so the confidence requirement at level \(\eta_1\) is at least as stringent as the one at level \(\eta_2\). Therefore

\(q_T(\eta_1)\ge q_T(\eta_2),\)

which means that _q<sub>T</sub>_ is nonincreasing as a function of \(\eta\).

Since _u<sub>T</sub>_ is also a upper-quantile bound, the definition of _q<sub>T</sub>_ gives

\(q_T(\eta)\le u_T(\eta)\forall\eta\in(0,1].\)

Hence

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_T(2^{-k})\le\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}u_T(2^{-k})<\infty.\)

This proves the claim.

**Lemma F.5** (Finite mean gives summable dyadic quantiles)**.** _Let_ \(X\ge 0\) _satisfy_ \(\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty\)_, and let_<tbc>

\(q_X(\eta):=inf\{x\ge 0:\mathbb{P}(X\le x)\ge 1-\eta\},\eta\in(0,1].\)

<tbc>_Then_

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_X(2^{-k})<\infty.\)

<tbc>_Proof of Lemma F.5._ The map \(\eta\mapsto q_X(\eta)\) is nonincreasing. For each \(k\ge 0\) and \(u\in[2^{-k-1},2^{-k}]\), one has \(q_X(u)\ge q_X(2^{-k})\). Hence<tbc>

\(2^{-k}q_X(2^{-k})\le 2\int_{2^{-k-1}}^{2^{-k}}q_X(u)du.\)

<tbc>Summing over _k_ and using the quantile representation of expectation gives

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_X(2^{-k})\le 2\int_0^1q_X(u)du=2\mathbb{E}[X]<\infty.\)

Since \(s<t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})\), at least one arm is separation-deficient. If some separation- deficient arm is not the current leader _B_<sub>_s_+1</sub>, then Lemma G.1 implies that the greedy challenger selected by the unguarded rule has count \(N_{s,C_{s+1}}<M_\eta\). Thus _X_<sub>_s_+1</sub>=1 whenever the challenger is pulled. If no separation-deficient nonleader exists, then every separation-deficient arm must be the current leader. In that case \(N_{s,B_{s+1}}<n_\star(\overline{\eta})\le M_\eta\), so _X_<sub>_s_+1</sub>=1 whenever the leader is pulled. In both cases,

\(\mathbb{E}[X_{s+1}|\mathcal{F}_s]\ge p\text{on}\mathcal{E}_\overline{\eta}\cap\{s<T_\eta\wedge\tau_M\wedge t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})\}.\) (G.1)

On \(\mathcal{E}_\overline{\eta}\cap\{t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})>T_\eta\}\), one also has \(\tau_M>T_\eta\), because \(\tau_M\le T_\eta\) would imply \(t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})\le\tau_M\le T_\eta\). \(\sum_{s=K}^{T_\eta-1}X_{s+1}=D_K-D_{T_\eta}<D_K=K(M_\eta-1).\)

<tbc>Consequently,

\(\mathcal{E}_\overline{\eta}\cap\{t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})>T_\eta\}\subseteq\left\{\sum_{s=K}^{T_\eta-1}Y_{s+1}\le-a_\eta\right\},a_\eta:=p(T_\eta-K)-K(M_\eta-1).\) (G.2)

By the definition of \(T_\eta\),<tbc>

\(T_\eta-K\ge\frac{2K}{p}(M_\eta-1)+\frac{16}{p^2}\mathrm{log}\frac{6}{\eta},\)

<tbc>so \(a_\eta\ge p(T_\eta-K)/2\). Azuma-Hoeffding gives<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}_\mu\left(\sum_{s=K}^{T_\eta-1}Y_{s+1}\le-a_\eta\right)\le\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{a_\eta^2}{2(T_\eta-K)}\right)\le\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{p^2(T_\eta-K)}{8}\right)\le\eta/6.\)

<tbc>Since \(\mathbb{P}_\mu(\mathcal{E}_\overline{\eta}^c)\le 2\overline{\eta}=\eta/3\), (G.2) yields

\(\mathbb{P}_\mu\left(t_\mathrm{sep}(\eta/6)>T_\eta\right)\le\eta/2.\)

Because \(T_\eta\) has the polynomial form stated in Lemma G.1, the first claim follows.

For the consequent statement, set \(\overline{\eta}:=\eta/12\) in the preceding high-probability entry argument. Then<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}_\mu\left(t_\mathrm{sep}(\overline{\eta})\le T_\overline{\eta}\right)\ge 1-\eta/4\)

<tbc>after changing the instance-dependent constants. Intersect this event with the armwise confidence event \(\mathcal{K}_\overline{\eta}\), which has probability at least \(1-\eta/12\), and with the leader-fraction event \(\mathcal{A}_{\eta/4}\) of Proposition F.1, which has probability at least \(1-\eta/4\). On the intersection, Proposition 6.1 implies<tbc>

\(B_{t+1}=i^\star\forall t\ge T_\overline{\eta}.\)

<tbc>Lemma F.2 then gives a _U_-stabilization time satisfying<tbc>

\(t_U\le C_{\beta,U}\left(T_\overline{\eta}+K+\mathrm{log}\frac{e(T_\overline{\eta}+1)^2}{\eta}\right).\)

<tbc>The failure probability of the intersection is at most

\(\eta/4+\eta/12+\eta/4<\eta.\)
