## G.3 Finite-mean sufficient exploration

_Proof of Theorem 6.4._ It is enough to construct a summable upper-quantile bound for a _U_- stabilization time _t<sub>U</sub>_, since the expectation bound then follows from Theorem 5.2.

Let<tbc>

\(q_\mathrm{se}(\xi):=\mathrm{inf}\{x\ge 0:\mathbb{P}_\mu(T_\mathrm{se}\le x)\ge 1-\xi\},\xi\in(0,1],\)

<tbc>be the upper-tail quantile of _T_<sub>se</sub>. By Lemma F.5,<tbc>

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_\mathrm{se}(2^{-k})<\infty.\)

<tbc>For \(\xi\in(0,1/2]\), set<tbc>

\(R_\xi:=\mathrm{log}\frac{K}{\xi}+\mathrm{loglog}\frac{e}{\xi}+1.\)

<tbc>Lemma E.5 gives \(n_\star(\xi)\le A_\mu R_\xi\). For \(\eta\in(0,1/4]\), define<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta):=q_\mathrm{se}(\eta/3)+\left[\frac{K}{c_\mathrm{se}^2}n_\star(\eta/3)^2\right]+1.\)

<tbc>On the event \(\{T_\mathrm{se}\le q_\mathrm{se}(\eta/3)\}\), every \(t\ge L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)\) satisfies \(t\ge T_\mathrm{se}\) and<tbc>

\(\mathrm{min}_iN_{t,i}\ge c_\mathrm{se}\sqrt{t/K}\ge n_\star(\eta/3).\)

<tbc>Hence \(t_\mathrm{sep}(\eta/3)\le L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)\). Intersecting this event with the armwise confidence event \(\mathcal{K}_{\eta/3}\), Proposition 6.1 implies<tbc>

\(B_{t+1}=i^\star\forall t\ge L_\mathrm{se}(\eta).\)

<tbc>Now also intersect with the event \(\mathcal{A}_{\eta/3}\) of Proposition F.1. Since the rule is unguarded, the guard term in Lemma F.2 is absent, and the lemma gives entry into the stabilized regime time satisfying

\(t_U\le u_U(\eta):=C_{\beta,U}\left(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)+\mathrm{log}\frac{e(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)+1)^2}{\eta/3}\right).\)

The three events used above have total probability at least \(1-\eta\). Thus _u<sub>U</sub>_ is a upper-quantile bound on (0,1/4]; extend it to (0,1] by setting \(u_U(\eta)=u_U(1/4)\) for \(\eta>1/4\).

It remains to check dyadic summability. Since \(n_\star(\eta)\le A_\mu R_\eta\),<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)\le q_\mathrm{se}(\eta/3)+C_{\mu,c_\mathrm{se},K}R_{\eta/3}^2.\)

<tbc>Along \(\eta_k=2^{-k}\), monotonicity of _q_<sub>se</sub> gives \(q_\mathrm{se}(2^{-k}/3)\le q_\mathrm{se}(2^{-k-2})\), and therefore<tbc>

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}q_\mathrm{se}(2^{-k}/3)<\infty.\)

<tbc>The dyadic sums of \(R_{2^{-k}/3}^2\) and log(_e/_2<sup>-_k_</sup>) are finite. Finally,<tbc>

\(\mathrm{log}\frac{e(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)+1)^2}{\eta/3}\le C\left(L_\mathrm{se}(\eta)+\mathrm{log}(e/\eta)+1\right),\)

<tbc>using \(\mathrm{log}(1+x)\le x\). Hence

\(\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-k}u_U(2^{-k})<\infty.\)

The expectation part of Theorem 5.2 now yields the displayed bound.

## G.4 All-distinct means instances

_Proof of Corollary 6.5._ For all-distinct Bernoulli instances, the bounded-reward theorem of Jourdan et al. \[9\], specialized to the EB leader and TCI challenger under their tie-breaking convention, proves the sufficient-exploration property used in their asymptotic \(\beta\)-optimality argument. In the Bernoulli/SPEF instantiation covered by their generic top-two analysis, this gives an almost sure finite random time _T_<sub>se</sub> with \(\mathbb{E}_\mu[T_\mathrm{se}]<\infty\) such that

\(\mathrm{min}_{i\in[K]}N_{t,i}\ge\sqrt{t/K}\forall t\ge T_\mathrm{se}.\)

Thus Theorem 6.4 applies with _c_<sub>se</sub>=1 to that tie-breaking variant. This corollary does not extend the cited sufficient-exploration result to the fixed deterministic tie-breaking convention used in Algorithm 1.

### G.5 Guarded expected bound

_Proof of Proposition 6.6._ Let \(m\ge 1\) and define epoch boundaries _t<sub>m</sub>=Km_<sup>2</sup>. By initialization, _N_<sub>_t_<sub>1</sub>_,i_</sub>=1 for all arms. Assume inductively that \(N_{t_m,i}\ge m\) for all arms. Consider any time \(t\in\{t_m,\dots,t_{m+1}-1\}\). Since \(\sqrt{t/K}<m+1\), the guard condition implies \(min_iN_{t,i}\le m\). Each time the guard triggers, it pulls a least-sampled arm. After at most _K_ such guard pulls, all arms satisfy \(N_{t,i}\ge m+1\). Because the interval length is \(t_{m+1}-t_m=K(2m+1)\ge K\), this happens no later than _t_<sub>_m_+1</sub>. The lower bound on min_<sub>i</sub>N<sub>t,i</sub>_ follows by induction. The bound on \(t_\mathrm{sep}(\eta)\) is immediate. The polylogarithmic upper-quantile bound for an _U_-stabilization time _t<sub>U</sub>_ follows by combining Lemma E.5, Proposition 6.1, Proposition F.1, and Lemma F.2.

_Proof of Theorem 6.7._ By Proposition 6.6 and Lemma F.2, the guard yields a polylogarithmic upper- quantile bound for a _U_-stabilization time _t<sub>U</sub>_. In particular, both the probability requirement and the dyadic summability condition in Theorem 5.2 hold. Applying the expectation part of Theorem 5.2 completes the proof.

### G.6 Limitation of one-step index comparisons

**Lemma G.2** (Asymptotics under a frozen wrong leader)**.** _Fix_ \(b\neq u\) _and counts_ \(m\ge 1\)_. Then the map_

\(n\mapsto\mathrm{inf}_{x\in(0,1)}\left\{nd(\mu_b,x)+md(\mu_u,x)\right\}\)

_is nondecreasing, and as_ \(n\rightarrow\infty\) _it converges to_ \(md(\mu_u,\mu_b)\).

_Proof of Lemma G.2._ Monotonicity in _n_ is immediate because the objective contains the nonnegative term \(nd(\mu_b,x)\). Evaluating at \(x=\mu_b\) gives the upper bound \(md(\mu_u,\mu_b)\). Conversely, let _x<sub>n</sub>_ be any sequence of near-minimizers. If \(d(\mu_b,x_n)\) failed to converge to zero, then the term \(nd(\mu_b,x_n)\) would diverge, contradicting the finite upper bound obtained by evaluating at \(x=\mu_b\). Hence \(x_n\rightarrow\mu_b\), and continuity gives the matching lower bound.

_Proof of Proposition 6.8._ Because \(\mu_j=\mu_b=\lambda\), choosing \(x=\lambda\) gives<tbc>

\(\Phi_j^{(b)}(n,M(\eta))=\mathrm{log}M(\eta)\)

<tbc>for every _n_. Fix any \(a<Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)\) and choose \(\varepsilon>0\) so that \(a<Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)-2\varepsilon\). By Lemma G.2, for every sufficiently small \(\eta\) there exists \(n_\eta\) such that for all \(n\ge n_\eta\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{inf}_x\left\{nd(\lambda,x)+m_u(\eta)d(\mu_u,x)\right\}\ge m_u(\eta)d(\mu_u,\lambda)-\varepsilon\mathrm{log}(e/\eta).\)

<tbc>Since \(m_u(\eta)\ge C\mathrm{log}(e/\eta)\) for small \(\eta\),<tbc>

\(\Phi_u^{(b)}(n,m_u(\eta))\ge(Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)-\varepsilon)\mathrm{log}(e/\eta)+\mathrm{log}m_u(\eta).\)

<tbc>By assumption, for all sufficiently small \(\eta\) and all \(n\ge n_\eta\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{log}M(\eta)=\Phi_j^{(b)}(n,M(\eta))\ge\Phi_u^{(b)}(n,m_u(\eta))\ge(Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)-\varepsilon)\mathrm{log}(e/\eta).\)

<tbc>Hence

\(M(\eta)\ge\eta^{-(Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)-\varepsilon)}.\)

Because \(a<Cd(\mu_u,\lambda)-2\varepsilon\), this implies \(M(\eta)\ge\eta^{-a}\) for all sufficiently small \(\eta\).

## H.1 Algorithms and implementation All variants use the same GLR stopping rule, the threshold \(c(t,\delta)=log(1/\delta)+2log(1+t/2)+2+log(K-1)\), and smallest-index deterministic tie-breaking. We compare three sampling variants: • **Unguarded penalized**: the original rule, with challenger \(C_{t+1}\in argmin_{j\neq B_{t+1}}\{W_t(B_{t+1},j)+logN_{t,j}\}\). • **Guarded penalized**: the same rule, except that if \(min_iN_{t,i}<\sqrt{t/K}\), the algorithm pulls a least-sampled arm. • **Unpenalized ablation**: the challenger minimizes _Wt(B__t_+1_,j_) instead of _Wt(B__t_+1_,j_)+log_Nt,j_; the stopping rule, threshold, initialization, and tie-breaking are unchanged. The implementation evaluates the Bernoulli two-sample GLR at the pooled mean, uses numba- accelerated simulation kernels, and records every run in a raw CSV with the stopping time, final recommendation, cap indicator, guard count, final arm counts, and optimal population weights. ### Computing the population benchmark and finite-confidence predictor For each instance and each \(\beta\), we compute \(T_\beta^\star(\mu)\) from the Bernoulli equalization system. For fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and challenger \(j\neq i^\star\), define \(I_j^\alpha(w)=inf_{x\in(0,1)}\{\alpha d(\mu_{i^\star},x)+wd(\mu_j,x)\},w>0.\) The optimizer is characterized by a scalar \(\lambda_\alpha\) such that \(I_j^\alpha(w_j^\alpha)=\lambda_\alpha\forall j\neq i^\star,\sum_{j\neq i^\star} w_j^\alpha=1-\alpha,\) and \(T_\alpha^\star(\mu)=1/\lambda_\alpha\).
